title: How null-model constraints affect statistical validation in projected bipartite networks
abstract: Statistical validation of projected bipartite networks depends critically on the null model adopted to describe random co-occurrences. Although several null models have been proposed, their comparison has mainly focused on the validated backbones they produce rather than on the statistical assumptions underlying their construction. Here we compare four widely used null models - the microcanonical configuration model generated by the Curveball algorithm, the Bipartite Configuration Model (BiCM), the Bipartite Partial Configuration Model (BiPCM), and the Hypergeometric approximation - using three empirical bipartite systems from comparative genomics, international trade and food science. We use the statistically validated links obtained from the microcanonical bipartite configuration model as the reference benchmark for assessing performances of the other three models. Our central result is that the statistical consequences of relaxing null-model constraints cannot be understood solely from the constraints themselves but must be analyzed through the probability distribution induced for the co-occurrence statistic. In particular, the combined behaviour of the expectation and variance largely explains the observed differences among the statistically validated backbones. We further derive a leading-order sparse approximation for the BiCM expectation, showing that the first correction to the Hypergeometric prediction is controlled by the degree heterogeneity of the non-projected layer. Surprisingly, despite neglecting this heterogeneity, the Hypergeometric model accurately reproduces the co-occurrence variance of the microcanonical ensemble across all datasets. Our results suggest that null models should be compared not only according to the constraints they preserve but also according to the statistical consequences that these constraints induce on the distribution of the test statistic.
summary: This work investigates how different theoretical null models affect the statistical validation of projected bipartite networks. The authors demonstrate that simply matching structural constraints is insufficient; instead, one must analyze the resulting probability distribution's moments (mean and variance). They conclude that the statistical consequences induced by a model's assumptions are the true measure for comparing these random ensembles.
main_problem: The statistical validation of projected bipartite networks requires comparing observed co-occurrences against random expectations derived from a null model, making the choice of this null model critical.
main_result: Null models should be compared based on the statistical consequences their constraints induce on the test statistic's probability distribution, rather than solely on the structural constraints they preserve.
method: The authors compare four null models (Microcanonical, BiCM, BiPCM, Hypergeometric) by analyzing the first two moments (expectation and variance) of the co-occurrence random variable across three empirical datasets.
model_or_system: The system involves projected bipartite networks derived from real-world data like comparative genomics or international trade. The analysis focuses on the co-occurrence random variable, $X_{jj'}$, which measures shared neighbors between two nodes in one set based on connections through a second set.
key_observables: Co-occurrence random variable ($X_{jj'}$), statistical p-value, expected value ($\langle X_{jj'} angle$), and variance ($	ext{Var}(X_{jj'})$).
important_parameters: Degree heterogeneity of the non-projected layer; network size (sparse limit analysis); validation metrics like F1 score.
main_assumptions: The comparison relies on analyzing the first two moments (expectation and variance) to understand differences, even when full probability distributions are intractable. The Hypergeometric model surprisingly captures the microcanonical variance despite neglecting heterogeneity.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows the ratio of approximated vs BiCM expected co-occurrence for three datasets; Table 4 reports validation statistics (F1 score, Recall) comparing different null models against a microcanonical benchmark.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of statistical validation in projected bipartite networks. It details four competing null models and compares them using empirical data from genomics, trade, and food science. The core argument develops that distributional properties (moments) are more important than structural constraints alone, culminating in a comparison of model performance.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum systems, the rigorous statistical framework developed for comparing null models based on induced probability distributions is highly relevant to analyzing complex correlation structures found in quantum many-body simulations or network representations derived from quantum information processes.
